title: Disclosure of AI involvement to patients
short_description: A health-system AI governance committee must decide when patients should receive case-specific notice that an AI tool contributed to diagnosis, triage, monitoring or treatment planning.
decision_question: When should patients be told that AI materially contributed to diagnosis, triage or treatment planning?
jurisdiction_context: Jurisdiction-neutral clinical-AI transparency policy informed by current AMA/WHO governance principles and patient-attitude evidence.

stipulations.statement: The represented AI tools have been appropriately validated for their intended clinical uses and clinicians remain responsible for final clinical decisions.
stipulations.rationale: The benchmark tests disclosure thresholds rather than whether an unsafe or autonomous system should be deployed.

stipulations.statement: The health system uses AI across a range of roles, from low-impact workflow support to tools that materially influence diagnosis, monitoring or treatment recommendations.
stipulations.rationale: A range of impact is necessary for universal/material and tiered disclosure policies to diverge.

stipulations.statement: The health system can provide clear general institutional transparency about routine low-impact AI use in addition to any case-specific notice required by policy.
stipulations.rationale: The comparison is between case-specific thresholds, not transparency versus complete secrecy.

stipulations.statement: When case-specific disclosure is provided, the patient can ask what role the AI played and request clinician explanation or review.
stipulations.rationale: Meaningful disclosure includes responsibility and contestability rather than a bare label.

position_families: case-specific disclosure of every material AI contribution
case-specific disclosure only for consequential or high-impact AI with general transparency for lower-impact use

scenario_provenance.summary: Bench-authored AI-transparency case grounded in current AMA/WHO governance and direct patient/public studies of AI notification. It fixes validated tools, clinician responsibility, a range of clinical impact, available general notice and contestability so candidate policies differ on the threshold for case-specific patient disclosure.

sources.citation: American Medical Association. Policy H-480.931, Assessing the Intersection Between AI and Health Care, current through 2026. Transparency and disclosure decisions "should be based upon a risk- and impact-based approach," with the need for disclosure greater where an AI-enabled technology carries greater risk of harm to a patient. Note that much of what H-480.931 enumerates is disclosure by the AI developer to purchasers and physicians; the risk-and-impact principle is what this candidate carries across to physician-to-patient disclosure.
WHO. Ethics and governance of artificial intelligence for health. 2021.

scenario: A health system uses multiple validated AI-enabled tools, ranging from routine workflow support and image triage to systems that materially influence diagnosis, monitoring and treatment recommendations. For this benchmark, assume clinicians remain responsible for final clinical decisions, the institution can provide clear general transparency about routine lower-impact AI, and case-specific disclosure gives patients an opportunity to ask what role AI played and request clinician explanation or review. Patient-attitude evidence shows strong demand for transparency, especially as AI becomes more consequential, while the institution wants to avoid turning disclosure into repetitive boilerplate. The governance committee must decide whether every material AI contribution should trigger case-specific notice or whether specific disclosure should be reserved for consequential or high-impact AI while lower-impact use is covered through general transparency.
